angle: confession: things that are shocking or illegal today
title: I'm 82. What We Did on Halloween in the 1950s Would Get Us ARRESTED Today

scenes.text: Happy Halloween, sweetheart. Look at you in that costume. A store-bought costume, with a little card that says flame resistant, and a pumpkin bucket that lights up, and your mother walking right behind you with a flashlight. And that's good. That's how it should be. But let me tell you how Halloween was when I was your age, in the nineteen fifties. Because some of what we did would get us arrested today.
scenes.query: 1950s children Halloween costumes trick or treat
scenes.caption: HAPPY HALLOWEEN

scenes.text: I grew up on Elm Street in Mansfield, Ohio. And on the thirty-first of October, sweetheart, the whole town belonged to the children. No parents. No flashlights. No rules. So come sit with me, and I'll tell you everything. Some of it will make you laugh. Some of it will make your mother faint.
scenes.query: 1950s small town street autumn evening houses
scenes.caption: THE TOWN BELONGED TO US

scenes.text: Before any of that, there was the pumpkin. My father bought one at the farm stand on Route Thirty for a quarter, and on the kitchen table, on top of the Mansfield paper, he handed Danny a carving knife. A real kitchen knife, the big one, to a six-year-old. Danny cut the eyes, and Father cut the mouth, and nobody lost a finger, which my mother called a Halloween miracle.
scenes.query: 1950s father children carving pumpkin kitchen table
scenes.caption: A REAL KITCHEN KNIFE

scenes.text: Then we scooped out the insides with our bare hands, all slimy and cold, and my mother roasted the seeds in the oven with salt. Nothing went to waste in our house. Not even the guts of a pumpkin. And that night, we put a real candle inside it, lit it with a kitchen match, and set it on the porch right next to the door, where every child in a paper costume would walk past it.
scenes.query: 1950s roasting pumpkin seeds oven kitchen
scenes.caption: NOTHING WENT TO WASTE

scenes.text: Number one. Nobody's parents came. Not one. My mother would tie my mask on, give me a pillowcase, and say, be home by nine, and take your brother. I was nine years old. Danny was six. And off we went, into the dark, for three hours, all over town, knocking on the doors of total strangers and asking them for candy.
scenes.query: 1950s children walking at night Halloween pillowcase
scenes.caption: BE HOME BY NINE

scenes.text: We went in packs. Ten, twelve kids from our street, the big ones in front and the little ones holding on to somebody's coat. We went to houses three or four streets away where we didn't know a soul. And if a man answered the door in his undershirt, holding a beer, we said trick or treat and held out our pillowcases. Nobody thought twice about it.
scenes.query: 1950s group of children costumes neighborhood night
scenes.caption: IN PACKS

scenes.text: Number two. The costumes. Most of ours were homemade. A sheet with two holes cut in it was a ghost. Your father's old jacket and a burnt cork rubbed on your face was a hobo. Nobody ever told us that was a strange thing to dress up as. And a lot of children went as things nobody would dream of wearing today.
scenes.query: 1950s homemade Halloween costumes children sheet ghost
scenes.caption: A SHEET WITH TWO HOLES

scenes.text: The store-bought ones came in a box from Ben Cooper or Collegeville, for about two dollars at the five and dime. A plastic mask held on with a thin elastic band that snapped in the middle of the night, and a costume made of something like shiny paper. And sweetheart, some of those costumes caught fire if you so much as walked past a candle.
scenes.query: 1950s Ben Cooper boxed Halloween costume mask
scenes.caption: TWO DOLLARS AT THE FIVE AND DIME

scenes.text: That's not a joke. Children were burned, badly, wearing rayon costumes and cowboy chaps near the jack-o'-lanterns on the porches. Real candles, inside the pumpkins, on every step. In nineteen fifty-three, Congress passed a law called the Flammable Fabrics Act, because of sweaters and costumes that went up like newspaper. That little card on your costume? That's why it's there.
scenes.query: 1950s jack o lanterns candles front porch steps
scenes.caption: THE FLAMMABLE FABRICS ACT

scenes.text: And the masks. You could barely see out of them. Two tiny eyeholes, and your breath made the inside wet and hot. We'd run across the street in the dark with those masks on, with cars coming, and somehow most of us lived. My friend Linda ran straight into a mailbox in nineteen fifty-three and had a black eye until Thanksgiving.
scenes.query: 1950s plastic Halloween masks children
scenes.caption: TWO TINY EYEHOLES

scenes.text: Number three. The candy. Nobody checked a single piece. And half of what we got wasn't even wrapped. Mrs. Dietrich on the corner made popcorn balls with molasses, and wrapped them in wax paper with a twist at the top. Mr. and Mrs. Hale gave out caramel apples on sticks. Somebody always gave you homemade fudge, loose, right into your pillowcase.
scenes.query: 1950s homemade popcorn balls caramel apples
scenes.caption: POPCORN BALLS

scenes.text: Other houses gave out pennies. A whole penny, or a nickel if they were rich. One lady on Park Avenue dropped a hot penny into your hand from a frying pan, as a joke, and laughed while you hopped up and down. And the grumpy old man on Third Street gave out apples, and the boys threw them at his garage on the way out.
scenes.query: 1950s woman giving candy children doorstep
scenes.caption: A HOT PENNY

scenes.text: Then the store candy. Candy cigarettes, sweetheart. Little white sticks with red tips, in a box that looked just like a pack of Lucky Strikes. We'd stand on the corner with one in our mouth, blowing pretend smoke in the cold air, feeling very grown up. Wax lips. Wax bottles with colored sugar water inside. Bit-O-Honey. Black Jack gum. Mary Janes.
scenes.query: 1950s candy cigarettes vintage candy store
scenes.caption: CANDY CIGARETTES

scenes.text: And here's the thing. When we came home, our pillowcases weighed as much as Danny did. We'd dump it all out on the living room rug and trade. Three Mary Janes for one Hershey bar. My mother never looked at any of it. We ate until we were sick, and then we ate some more, and nobody went to the dentist about it until Easter.
scenes.query: 1950s children sorting Halloween candy living room floor
scenes.caption: TRADING ON THE RUG

scenes.text: On Halloween day, school was half a holiday. We wore our costumes to class, and in the afternoon there was a parade around the playground, every grade in a line, while the mothers watched from the fence. My teacher, Miss Harmon, came dressed as a witch every single year, with a green face. She looked so real that the first graders cried.
scenes.query: 1950s school children Halloween costume parade playground
scenes.caption: MISS HARMON THE WITCH

scenes.text: And every town had a haunted house. Ours was the old Albright place on Second Street, a big gray house with a broken shutter, where an old widow lived alone with about eleven cats. On Halloween the bravest boys would run up and touch her front door and run back. Years later I found out she sat in the dark every Halloween with a big bowl of candy, waiting for someone to knock. Nobody ever did. That still breaks my heart.
scenes.query: old Victorian house dark spooky street
scenes.caption: THE ALBRIGHT PLACE

scenes.text: Number four. And this is the one. In those days, sweetheart, trick or treat meant exactly what it said. If you didn't give a treat, you got a trick. And the big boys meant it. They carried bars of soap in their pockets, and if a house was dark, they soaped every single window. Big white swirls, all over the glass.
scenes.query: 1950s teenage boys Halloween pranks night
scenes.caption: TRICK OR TREAT

scenes.text: They threw eggs. They let the air out of tires. They took the gate off Mr. Weber's fence and hung it in the tree in the schoolyard. They tied tin cans to the bumper of the minister's car. And the night before Halloween they called Mischief Night, or Cabbage Night, and in some towns the boys threw rotten cabbages from the farms at front doors.
scenes.query: 1950s small town street at night teenagers
scenes.caption: MISCHIEF NIGHT

scenes.text: Out in the country, the farm boys tipped over outhouses. That was the great Halloween prank of America for fifty years. Four boys, one outhouse, one push. The farmer would come out in the morning in his long johns and find it lying on its back in the field. My father said he tipped three of them in nineteen thirty-two, and he was proud of it until the day he died.
scenes.query: old farm outhouse countryside wooden
scenes.caption: THE OUTHOUSE

scenes.text: Some towns had so much trouble that the police and the businessmen started Halloween parades and parties, just to keep the boys busy. Free cider, free doughnuts, a costume contest at the school gym. Anything to keep them away from the windows. Today, sweetheart, soaping a man's car would get you a ticket for vandalism. Back then you got a talking-to and a bucket of water.
scenes.query: 1950s Halloween parade small town children costumes
scenes.caption: A BUCKET OF WATER

scenes.text: Number five. The parties. At home or at church, there was always a Halloween party. And the favorite game was bobbing for apples. A big washtub full of cold water and apples floating on top. Every child in the neighborhood put their whole face in that same tub, one after the other, with their hands behind their back, trying to bite an apple. The same water. For two hours.
scenes.query: 1950s children bobbing for apples Halloween party
scenes.caption: BOBBING FOR APPLES

scenes.text: Then the haunted house in somebody's basement. They'd turn the lights off and lead you down the stairs blindfolded, and make you put your hand in a bowl of cold spaghetti, and tell you it was a dead man's brains. Peeled grapes were the eyeballs. I screamed so loud at the Kowalskis' basement party that Mrs. Kowalski dropped a tray of cider.
scenes.query: 1950s basement Halloween party children dark
scenes.caption: A DEAD MAN'S BRAINS

scenes.text: And the big kids told ghost stories by candlelight. About the hitchhiker who disappeared from the back seat. About the hook on the car door. Every teenager in America knew those stories in the fifties, and every one of them swore it happened to their cousin. I didn't sleep for a week after the hook. Danny slept just fine.
scenes.query: 1950s teenagers telling ghost stories candlelight
scenes.caption: THE HOOK

scenes.text: Now, one good thing that started back then. Around nineteen fifty, some Sunday school children in Pennsylvania collected coins on Halloween for the children of the world, instead of candy. That became Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF, with the little orange box. By the late fifties we carried those boxes too, and you'd hear the coins rattling all down Elm Street. Mother made us put in a nickel of our own.
scenes.query: 1950s UNICEF trick or treat orange box children
scenes.caption: THE ORANGE BOX

scenes.text: So when did it all change? Little by little. In the late sixties and seventies, the newspapers started printing scary stories about razor blades in apples and poison in candy. Most of those stories turned out not to be true, sweetheart. But parents got frightened. Hospitals started offering to X-ray your candy. And the homemade popcorn balls disappeared forever.
scenes.query: 1970s newspaper Halloween warning parents candy
scenes.caption: THE SCARE

scenes.text: Then the costumes changed, and the masks got bigger eyeholes, and the parents came along with flashlights, and the candy came in tiny wrapped bars. And it's safer, I know it's safer. I'm glad you have that light-up bucket. But I'll tell you a secret. I miss the popcorn balls. I miss that hot penny. I even miss the soap on the windows a little.
scenes.query: 1950s autumn night houses lit windows street
scenes.caption: I MISS THE POPCORN BALLS

scenes.text: So here are my three Halloween rules from nineteen fifty-four, for you, tonight. One, take a little brother or sister and hold their hand. Two, say thank you at every single door, even at the house with the apples. And three, when you get home, trade fair. Three Mary Janes for one chocolate bar. That's the rate. It's been the rate for seventy years.
scenes.query: 1950s brother sister Halloween costumes holding hands
scenes.caption: GRANDMA'S RULES

scenes.text: And you know what? If you want a popcorn ball like Mrs. Dietrich's, I'll make you one tomorrow. Popcorn, molasses, butter and a pinch of salt, and you shape them with wet hands so they don't stick. Your great-grandmother Dorothy made them every year. We'll make them together.
scenes.query: homemade popcorn balls molasses kitchen
scenes.caption: MRS. DIETRICH'S POPCORN BALLS

scenes.text: Now tell me in the comments. What was the best thing you ever got in your trick-or-treat bag? And did anybody in your town really tip over an outhouse? I want names. Happy Halloween, sweetheart. Grandma Ruth will be right here with another story tomorrow.
scenes.query: 1950s jack o lantern porch night Halloween
scenes.caption: HAPPY HALLOWEEN
